body:
Real Ketchup wrote...
> Anyway, if I were to hold the New York Times hostage, I would have
> them publish Bertrand Russell's "The Conquest of Happiness" and
> B. F. Skinner's "Walden Two" -- the former outlining the sort of
> changes necessary for individuals and the latter those for societies.
> (To properly understand "Walden Two", mentally replace all behaviorist
> language with your preferred psychological jargon).

B.F. Skinner was a dangerous fraud.  I learned about his so-called
theory of behaviorism in college and while I reject all fields of
the pseudo-science of psychology, his seems especially dangerous.

His crackpot theory led to the psychological torture of a boy who
suffered penile mutilation during circumcision.  The doctors had
to amputate his penis but since they had watched an episode of Dr.
Phil (oops, I mean Dr. Skinner), they were experts on behaviorism
and assured the parents that all they had to do is raise him as a
female and he would become female, because gender is solely a
result of social training.

Of course he didn't become a girl, he became a boy in a dress who
liked to play with toy soldiers and trucks and all that, and when
he hit puberty he was further traumatized by the though he might
be homosexual when he began being attracted to girls.  Eventually
he learned the truth, changed his gender back to male as much as
was possible, and committed suicide a year or two ago.  And you
have the nerve to compare the charlatan Skinner's writings to
anything St. Ted wrote.

Oh, and I might add that yesterday's newspaper carried a story on
an experiment at Texas A&M (I think) with 88 monkeys (44 male and
44 female).  From birth they gave the monkeys various human toys
and carefully observed how much time they played with each toy.
With no human influence, the boy monkeys preferred toy cars and
throwing balls and the girl monkeys preferred to play with dolls.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
"The trouble with such theorists is that they have made the development and
application of social theories their surrogate activity.  Consequently the
theories are designed to serve the needs of the theorists more than the
needs of any people who may be unlucky enough to live in a society on which
the theories are imposed."
-- St. Ted
